source_text: Nec ideo tamen contemnenda et abicienda sunt corpora defunctorum maximeque iustorum atque fidelium, quibus tamquam organis et uasis ad omnia bona opera sancte usus est spiritus. si enim paterna uestis et anulus ac si quid huius modi tanto carius est posteris, quanto erga parentes maior affectus, nullo modo ipsa spernenda sunt corpora, quae utique multo familiarius atque coniunctius quam quaelibet indumenta gestamus. haec enim non ad ornamentum uel adiutorium, quod adhibetur extrinsecus, sed ad ipsam naturam hominis pertinent. unde et antiquorum iustorum funera officiosa pietate curata sunt et exequiae celebratae et sepultura prouisa, ipsique, cum uiuerent, de sepeliendis uel etiam transferendis suis corporibus filiis mandauerunt. et Tobis sepeliendo mortuos deum promeruisse teste angelo commendatur. ipse quoque dominus die tertio resurrecturus religiosae mulieris bonum opus praedicat praedicandumque commendat. quod unguentum pretiosum super membra eius effuderit atque hoc ad eum sepeliendum fecerit. et laudabiliter commemorantur in euangelio qui corpus eius de cruce acceptum diligenter atque honorifice tegendum sepeliendumque curarunt. uerum istae auctoritates non hoc admonent, quod insit ullus cadaueribus sensus, sed ad dei prouidentiam, cui placent etiam talia pietatis officia, corpora quoque mortuorum pertinere significant propter fidem resurrectionis astruendam. ubi et illud salubriter discitur, quanta possit esse remuneratio pro elemosynis, quas uiuentibus et sentientibus exhibemus, si neque hoc apud deum perit, quod exanimis hominum membris officii diligentiaeque persoluitur. sunt quidem et alia, quae sancti patriarchae de corporibus suis uel condendis uel transferendis prophetico spiritu dicta intellegi uoluerunt; non autem hic locus est, ut ea pertractemus, cum sufficiant ista quae diximus. sed si ea quae sustentandis uiuentibus sunt necessaria, sicut uictus et amictus, quamuis cum graui afflictione desint, non frangunt in bonis perferendi tolerandique uirtutem nec eradicant ex animo pietatem, sed exercitatam faciunt fecundiorem: quanto magis, cum desunt ea, quae curandis funeribus condendisque corporibus defunctorum adhiberi solent, non efficiunt miseros in occultis piorum sedibus iam quietos! ac per hoc, quando ista cadaueribus Christianorum in illa magnae urbis uel etiam aliorum oppidorum uastatione defuerunt, nec uiuorum culpa est, qui non potuerunt ista praebere, nec poena mortuorum, qui non possunt ista sentire\\ haec est mea de sepulturae causa atque ratione sententia. quam propterea ex alio libro meo in istum transtuli, quia facilius hoc a me recenseri potuit, quam\' id ipsum alio modo eloquendum fuit.
thought_title: Bodies of the dead are not to be despised, because they belong to human nature and to God's providence
orientation: Augustine is answering Paulinus's question about burial, and here he argues that although burial does not help the dead directly, the bodies of the dead, especially the faithful, are not to be despised.
pass_a_gloss: And yet for this reason the bodies of the dead are not to be despised and cast away, especially of the just and of the faithful, which the spirit used as instruments and vessels for all good works in a holy way. For if a father's garment and ring and anything of this kind is so much dearer to descendants, the greater the affection toward parents, in no way are those bodies themselves to be despised, which certainly we wear much more closely and more intimately than any garments. For these do not pertain to ornament or to help, which is applied from outside, but to the very nature of man. Hence also the funerals of the just of old were cared for with dutiful piety, and funeral rites were celebrated, and burial was provided, and they themselves, while they lived, commanded their sons about burying or even about transferring their bodies. And Tobit is commended, with the angel as witness, to have merited God by burying the dead. The Lord himself also, about to rise on the third day, proclaims the good work of the religious woman and commends it as something to be proclaimed, that she poured precious ointment over his limbs and did this for burying him. And they are praised in the gospel who took his body from the cross and carefully and honorably saw to covering and burying it. But these authorities do not warn this, that there is any sensation in corpses, but they signify that the bodies of the dead also pertain to the providence of God, to whom even such offices of piety are pleasing, for the sake of building up faith in the resurrection. Where also this is learned in a salutary way, how great can be the reward for alms which we show to the living and to those who feel, if not even this perishes before God, which is paid to the lifeless limbs of men by the office of care and diligence. There are also other things which the holy patriarchs said about burying or transferring their bodies, which they wanted to be understood in a prophetic spirit; but this is not the place to treat them, since the things which we have said are sufficient. But if the things which are necessary for sustaining the living, such as food and clothing, although they are lacking with grave affliction, do not break in good men the virtue of enduring and tolerating, and do not root out piety from the soul, but make it more fruitful by exercise: how much more, when the things are lacking which are usually applied to caring for funerals and burying the bodies of the dead, do they not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious! And through this, when those things were lacking for the corpses of Christians in that devastation of the great city or even of other towns, neither is it the fault of the living, who could not provide those things, nor the punishment of the dead, who cannot feel those things. This is my opinion about the cause and reason of burial. Which for this reason I transferred from another book of mine into this one, because it could more easily be reviewed by me than the same thing had to be expressed in another way.

choices.why: Keeps the sense of formal, owed care (officiosa) joined to religious devotion (pietate), matching Augustine's point that burial is a duty of affection.

choices.english: for the sake of building up faith in the resurrection
choices.why: Astruendam means constructing or establishing; 'building up' preserves the active, edifying force Augustine intends.
rejected: to confirm faith in the resurrection

choices.term: in occultis piorum sedibus iam quietos
choices.english: already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious
choices.why: Keeps the spatial and hidden quality of occultis sedibus and the perfect passive sense of quietos, avoiding any suggestion of a named place like 'hell'.
rejected: in the secret resting places of the godly
in the hidden dwellings of the faithful

choices.why: Exanimis means without breath or life; 'lifeless limbs' preserves the physical, bodily focus Augustine contrasts with the living and feeling.
Officium here is the dutiful service of burial; diligentia is the attentiveness. The pair captures both the obligation and the carefulness.

pass_b_english: Yet we must not for that reason despise and cast aside the bodies of the dead, especially of the just and faithful, which the spirit used as instruments and vessels for every good work in a holy way. If a father's cloak and ring, or anything of that kind, is all the dearer to his descendants as their affection for their parents is greater, then in no way should the bodies themselves be despised, since we wear them far more closely and intimately than any clothing. For these do not belong to ornament or assistance applied from outside, but to the very nature of a human being. That is why the funerals of the righteous of old were attended with dutiful piety, their funeral rites were celebrated, and burial was provided for them; and while they were still alive they instructed their sons about burying or even transferring their bodies. Tobit is commended, on the testimony of an angel, as having merited God's favor by burying the dead (Tobit 12:12). The Lord himself, who was to rise on the third day, praises the good work of a religious woman and commends it for proclamation, because she poured precious ointment over his limbs and did it for his burial (Matthew 26:12-13). And the Gospel speaks with praise of those who took his body down from the cross and carefully and honorably saw to its wrapping and burial (John 19:38-40). But these authorities do not teach that there is any sensation in corpses. Rather, they show that the bodies of the dead also belong to God's providence, which is pleased even by such offices of piety, for the sake of building up faith in the resurrection. There we also learn a salutary lesson: how great the reward can be for the alms we offer to the living and feeling, if what is paid to the lifeless limbs of men in care and diligence does not perish before God. There are other things too which the holy patriarchs said about the burying or transferring of their bodies that they wished to be understood in a prophetic spirit, but this is not the place to discuss them, since what we have said is enough. But if the things necessary for sustaining the living, such as food and clothing, even when they are lacking with heavy affliction, do not break the virtue of enduring and bearing in good people, nor root piety out of the soul, but make it more fruitful through exercise: how much more, when the things customarily used for tending funerals and burying the bodies of the dead are lacking, they do not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious! And so, when these things were lacking for the corpses of Christians in the devastation of that great city or of other towns, it was neither the fault of the living, who could not provide them, nor the punishment of the dead, who cannot feel them. This is my judgment about the cause and reason of burial. I have transferred it here from another book of mine because it was easier for me to review it than to express the same thing in another way.

problems.quote: the good work of a devout woman
problems.why: Source says 'religious woman,' not 'devout woman'; 'religious' has specific connotation in context.
problems.fix: the good work of a religious woman

edits.old: the good work of a devout woman
edits.new: the good work of a religious woman

fixed: Changed 'devout woman' to 'religious woman' to match source 'religiosae mulieris'.

problems.quote: how much more, when the things customarily used for tending funerals and burying the bodies of the dead are lacking, do they not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious!
problems.source_quote: quanto magis, cum desunt ea, quae curandis funeribus condendisque corporibus defunctorum adhiberi solent, non efficiunt miseros in occultis piorum sedibus iam quietos!
problems.why: The English inverts the rhetorical force. The Latin says 'how much more... do they NOT make wretched' — the things lacking for funerals do NOT make wretched those at rest. The English 'do they not make wretched' is a question expecting 'yes', but the Latin 'non efficiunt miseros' is a strong negation: they DO NOT make them wretched. The 'non' is dropped or obscured.
problems.fix: how much more, when the things customarily used for tending funerals and burying the bodies of the dead are lacking, do they not render wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious!
problems.ruling: 'non efficiunt miseros' = they DO NOT make wretched. English 'do they not make wretched' is a question implying opposite, flipping meaning.

problems.quote: do they not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious!
problems.source_quote: non efficiunt miseros in occultis piorum sedibus iam quietos
problems.why: The 'non' before 'efficiunt' makes this a statement that they DO NOT make them wretched, not a rhetorical question. The English question form 'do they not' completely flips the meaning — it suggests they DO make them wretched.
problems.fix: they do not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious!
problems.ruling: 'non efficiunt miseros' = strong negation, not rhetorical question. English 'do they not' inverts meaning, misleading reader.

last_rejected.quote: Tobit is commended, on the testimony of an angel, as having merited God's favor by burying the dead (Tobit 12:12)
last_rejected.source_quote: et Tobis sepeliendo mortuos deum promeruisse teste angelo commendatur
last_rejected.why: Wrong scripture reference: Augustine cites Tobit burying the dead, not Tobit 12:12 specifically. The angel's testimony about alms/mercy is in Tobit 12:8-9, but the commendation for burying the dead is narrative in Tobit 1:17-20; 2:3-7.
last_rejected.fix: Tobit is commended, on the testimony of an angel, as having merited God by burying the dead.
last_rejected.ruling: Tobit 12:12 is a reasonable shorthand for angel's testimony; not a major misleading error.

last_rejected.quote: praises the good work of a religious woman and commends it for proclamation
last_rejected.source_quote: religiosae mulieris bonum opus praedicat praedicandumque commendat
last_rejected.why: Agency and sense shifted: 'praedicat' means he preaches/proclaims it (himself), not 'commends it for proclamation' by others. Jesus both praises and preaches the deed.
last_rejected.fix: praises the good work of a religious woman and preaches it, commending it to be preached.
last_rejected.ruling: 'praedicandumque commendat' reasonably supports 'commends it for proclamation'; within normal range.

last_rejected.quote: how great the reward can be for the alms we offer to the living and feeling
last_rejected.source_quote: quanta possit esse remuneratio pro elemosynis, quas uiuentibus et sentientibus exhibemus
last_rejected.why: Wrong sense: 'exhibemus' here means 'we show/display' (our care/diligence), not 'offer alms.' The point is showing care to living people, not giving alms to them.
last_rejected.fix: how great the reward can be for the alms, when we show them to the living and feeling.
last_rejected.ruling: 'elemosynis exhibemus' naturally reads 'alms we offer'; standard rendering, not a major error.

last_rejected.quote: what is paid to the lifeless limbs of men in care and diligence does not perish before God
last_rejected.source_quote: quod exanimis hominum membris officii diligentiaeque persoluitur
last_rejected.why: Wrong sense: 'persoluitur' means 'is performed/rendered,' not 'paid.' The care and diligence are rendered/performed, not paid as wages.
last_rejected.fix: what is rendered to the lifeless limbs of men in duty and diligence does not perish before God.
last_rejected.ruling: 'persoluitur' can mean 'paid/rendered'; 'paid' here means rendered, not wages; not misleading.

last_rejected.quote: they do not make wretched those already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious
last_rejected.source_quote: non efficiunt miseros in occultis piorum sedibus iam quietos
last_rejected.why: Wrong syntax: 'miseros' goes with 'efficiunt,' not 'quietos.' The dead are 'already at rest'; the lack of burial doesn't make them wretched. 'Quietos' is predicate, not 'miseros.'
last_rejected.fix: they do not make wretched those who are already at rest in the hidden abodes of the pious.
last_rejected.ruling: 'non efficiunt miseros...quietos' = 'do not make wretched those already at rest'; syntax correctly handled.
